query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a lubricious secondary phase (such as tungsten disulfide or an oxide that forms a lubricious layer at high temperatures) into a tungsten‐based refractory high‐entropy alloy will yield a self‐lubricating material that retains its high mechanical strength while reducing friction over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g. W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf) with a microstructure designed for high strength via coherent nanoprecipitations.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition or processing to introduce a secondary phase (e.g., nano-scale tungsten disulfide particles or alloying elements that promote formation of a lubricious oxide layer) into the RHEA matrix.
generation.conditions: Tested under a wide temperature range (from ambient up to elevated temperatures typical of high-temperature applications, e.g., 800 °C to 1600 °C) in environments that simulate extreme operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates or in-situ formed tribolayers at the alloy surface that act as solid lubricants
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the secondary phase either remains stable or transforms to form a continuous lubricious film (for instance, via the formation of tungsten disulfide or a thin oxide layer) that reduces friction and wear, while the high-entropy alloy matrix retains structural integrity and mechanical strength through its coherent nanoprecipitate microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The composite material will exhibit lower friction coefficients and improved wear resistance (i.e., self-lubrication) across the wide temperature range while maintaining high strength, compared to the baseline tungsten-based RHEA without lubricant-phase modification.
generation.baseline: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy without the intentionally introduced lubricious phase.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of self-lubrication may depend on the stability of the lubricious phase under specific environmental conditions (e.g., oxidizing vs reducing atmospheres) and may be limited by the precise temperature range where the lubricious film is stable.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, phase stability, and effectiveness of the lubricious film at different temperatures require experimental validation; the size and continuity of the lubricious phase and its interaction with the matrix under thermal cycling remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys with the lubricious secondary phase introduced (via alloying additions and processing to promote in-situ formation of a lubricious film) and an otherwise identical baseline sample without the additive. Subject both sets to tribological testing under controlled high-temperature conditions that span the intended operational range. Monitor friction coefficients, wear rates, and mechanical strength over time.
measurements: Wear rate and wear scar analysis via microscopy
Mechanical strength measurements before and after tribological testing
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS or Raman) to detect formation of lubricious phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the lubricious-phase-enhanced RHEA does not exhibit a significantly lower friction coefficient and improved wear resistance while retaining comparable mechanical strength compared to the baseline, or if the lubricious film does not form and remain stable across the target temperature range, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering
